title: Container Image Build Pipelines
summary: The CI-side mechanics that turn source into a fast-to-build, trustworthy, cacheable container image.

slides.markdown:
Every CI run rebuilding a container image from scratch is slow and wasteful — most layers (base image, OS packages, dependencies) don't change between commits. CI systems exploit Docker's layer cache the same way a local build does, but the cache has to be **persisted between runs**, since CI runners are often ephemeral.

Common approaches: a registry-backed cache (`--cache-from` pulling the previous image as a cache source) or a CI-native cache volume. Without one of these, a fresh runner rebuilds every layer every time, turning a 20-second build into a 5-minute one.

How you tag a built image determines whether anyone can later answer "what's actually running."

| Tag style | What it gives you | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Commit SHA | Exact, traceable to one commit | Not human-friendly to read off a dashboard |
| Semantic version (`v2.3.1`) | Meaningful to humans, ties to a release | Requires a separate versioning/release process |
| `latest` | Convenient to reference | Mutable — the same tag points to different bits over time |

**How to decide:** tag every build with the immutable commit SHA always, and layer semantic versions or `latest` as *additional*, human-friendly aliases on top — never as the only tag.

Pushing isn't just "upload the layers." A production pipeline handles three things the happy path glosses over: **authentication** (the CI runner needs scoped, often short-lived, registry credentials), **retries** (a push failing silently mid-pipeline is worse than a slow retry), and **multi-arch builds** (if the fleet runs both `amd64` and `arm64` nodes, the pipeline must push a manifest list covering both, not just the runner's own arch).

Skipping multi-arch support quietly breaks deploys the day someone adds an `arm64` node pool.

A build pipeline is the cheapest place to catch a known-CVE base image or dependency — before it ever reaches a registry a deploy pipeline trusts. A scanner (Trivy, Grype, or a cloud-native equivalent) runs against the freshly built image, and the pipeline **fails the build** on criticial/high findings above an agreed threshold.

The gate has to be tuned: too strict (fail on every low-severity finding) trains teams to ignore or bypass it; too loose defeats the purpose. Most teams gate on critical/high only and track medium/low separately.

slides.sectionTitle: A build-scan-push job, only pushing clean
slides.markdown:
A CI job that only pushes an image past a clean scan:

```yaml
build-and-scan:
  script:
    - docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA --cache-from $IMAGE:cache .
    - trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH $IMAGE:$SHA
    - docker push $IMAGE:$SHA   # only reached if trivy exits 0
```

`trivy`'s non-zero exit code stops the job before `push` ever runs — a vulnerable image never reaches the registry that the deploy pipeline trusts.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: the uncached build that makes CI crawl
slides.markdown:
A common failure mode: a Dockerfile that reinstalls every OS package on every run because the cache was never wired up, or was invalidated by a frequently-changing `COPY . .` placed before the dependency-install step. Every run pays the full cold-build cost — often minutes where a cached build takes seconds.

The fix: order Dockerfile instructions so rarely-changing layers come first (see the Dockerfile best-practices Topic), and make sure CI actually persists a cache between runs instead of starting cold each time.

slides.sectionTitle: Multi-stage builds and final image size
slides.markdown:
A naive Dockerfile ships the compiler, build tools, and source tree in the same image that runs in production — often turning a 50MB runtime into an 800MB+ image. A **multi-stage build** splits this: an early stage compiles or installs dependencies, and a final `FROM` stage copies only the built artifact into a minimal base.

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o app .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12
COPY --from=build /src/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

Smaller final images pull faster (fewer bytes over the network on every node that schedules a Pod), start faster, and — because there's no shell, package manager, or compiler in a distroless image — carry a smaller attack surface if the container is ever compromised.

slides.sectionTitle: Signing and provenance: proving what's in the image
slides.markdown:
Scanning catches known CVEs, but it doesn't prove an image is the one your pipeline actually built. **Image signing** (Cosign/Sigstore) lets the pipeline cryptographically sign a pushed image, and the deploy step (or an admission controller in the cluster) can refuse to run anything unsigned or signed by the wrong identity.

Alongside signing, a pipeline can emit an **SBOM** (software bill of materials) — a manifest of every package and version baked into the image — and a **provenance attestation** describing which source commit, builder, and steps produced it. Together these answer a question scanning alone can't: not just "does this image have known vulnerabilities," but "did this image really come from our pipeline, unmodified."

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: a cache that lies
slides.markdown:
Layer caching assumes a cache hit means "identical inputs, identical output" — but a cache key based only on a `COPY` step's file hash misses inputs that live outside the build context: a base image tag that moved (`node:20` pointing at a new patch release), a package registry serving a different version for an unpinned dependency, or a build arg that changes behavior without changing any file.

A staff engineer treats **unpinned upstream inputs** as the real risk, not the cache mechanism itself: pin base images by digest (`node:20@sha256:...`) and lockfile every dependency, so a cache hit and a cold build are provably the same artifact either way. Otherwise "reproducible" builds quietly stop being reproducible the moment an upstream tag moves under you.
